{{Short description|American mathematician, professor and author of textbooks}}
'''Neal Henry McCoy''' (March 6, 1905 – January 5, 2001) was an American [[mathematician]], university professor, and author of several textbooks for mathematics undergraduates. His 1960 textbook ''Introduction to Modern Algebra'' has gone through several editions and has been translated into many foreign languages.<ref name=papers>{{cite web|url=https://findingaids.smith.edu/repositories/4/resources/269 |title=Collection: Neal McCoy papers &#124; Smith College Finding Aids }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
McCoy was born into a homesteading family in [[Waukomis, Oklahoma]] (which was part of the [[Oklahoma Territory]] from 1890 to 1907). He had an older sister [[Dorothy McCoy]] (1903–2001), who became the first woman to receive a Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[University of Iowa]]. As an infant, he moved in 1906 with his mother and sister to [[Chesapeake, Missouri]] after the death of his father.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Green|first1=Judy|author1-link=Judy Green (mathematician)|last2=LaDuke|first2=Jeanne|author2-link=Jeanne LaDuke|contribution=McCoy, Dorothy, August 9, 1903 – November 21, 2001|date=January 2009|pages=240–241|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|title=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's|title-link=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IRbOAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA240}} Reprinted in {{cite web|url=http://unger.myplainview.com/supplement.pdf|title=From Apples to WACS: A Supplement to the Second Edition of ''Hale County, Texas, Bibliography''|first=John|last=Sigwald|date=January 2016|pages=S52–S53|publisher=Unger Memorial Library|location=Plain view, Texas|access-date=2020-03-25}} See also more detailed biography on pp. 399–401 of [https://www.ams.org/bookpages/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf Supplementary material for ''Pioneering Women in American Mathematics''].</ref> After graduating with a bachelor's degree from [[Baylor University]],<ref name=papers/> he became a graduate student at the [[University of Iowa]]. There he graduated in 1929 with a Ph.D. in mathematics with adviser Edward Wilson Chittenden. McCoy's Ph.D. thesis ''On commutation formulas in the algebra of quantum mechanics''<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=43113|name=Neal Henry McCoy}}</ref> was published in abbreviated form in the ''[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1929-1501512-1 |title=On commutation formulas in the algebra of quantum mechanics |date=1929 |last1=McCoy |first1=Neal H. |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=31 |issue=4 |pages=793–806 }}</ref>

==Career==
For two academic years from 1929 to 1931, McCoy studied at [[Princeton University]] as a National Research Fellow. He joined in 1931 the staff of the mathematics department of [[Northampton, Massachusetts|Northampton]]'s [[Smith College]],<ref name=papers/> There he was promoted to full professor in 1942<ref name=PMEJ>{{cite journal|title=Neal Henry McCoy, Associate Editor|journal=Pi Mu Epsilon Journal |date=April 1952|volume=1|issue=6|page=230|url=https://www.pme-math.org/journal/issues/PMEJ.Vol.1.No.6.pdf}}</ref> and was appointed to the Gates Chair in Mathematics in 1963, retiring as professor emeritus in 1970.<ref name=papers/> McCoy did research on [[abstract algebra]], especially the theory of [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]s and [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] with elements in rings, and algebraic aspects of quantum mechanics.<ref name=PMEJ/> From 1951 to 1954 he was the editor-in-chief of the ''[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]''.<ref name=papers/> He was an associate editor for the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'' and the [[Pi Mu Epsilon|''Pi Mu Epsilon Journal'']].<ref name=PMEJ/>

==McCoy ring==
In 1942, McCoy proved the following theorem:<br>Let R be a [[commutative ring]] with multiplicative unit, and let f(x) be a [[zero divisor]] in the [[polynomial ring]] R[x]. Then there is a nonzero element r ∈ R with f(x)r = 0.<ref>{{cite journal|author=McCoy, N. H.|title=Remarks on divisors of zero|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|volume=49|pages=286–295|year=1942|issue=5 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1942.11991226 }}</ref><br> In 1997 Mangesh B. Rege and Sima Chhawchharia introduced definitions of rings,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Rege, M. B.|author2=Chhawchharia, S.|title=Armendariz rings|journal=Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A Math. Sci.|volume=73|year=1997|issue=1|pages=14–17|doi=10.3792/pjaa.73.14 }}</ref> which in 2006, independently and motivated by McCoy's 1942 theorem, were re-introduced by Pace P. Nielsen, who gave the concepts the names "right McCoy ring", "left McCoy ring", and "McCoy ring" (a ring which is both right McCoy and left McCoy).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Nielsen, Pace P.|year=2006|title=Semi-commtativity and the McCoy condition|journal=Journal of Algebra|volume=298|issue=1|pages=134–141|doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2005.10.008 |url=http://www.math.byu.edu/~pace/McCoy_web.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=J. Korean Math. Soc.|volume=50|year=2013|issue=5|pages=959–972|url= http://dx.doi.org/10.4134/JKMS.2013.50.5.959|title=On a generalization of McCoy rings|author=Camillo, Victor|author2=Kwak, Tai Keun|author3=Lee, Yang|doi=10.4134/JKMS.2013.50.5.959 }}</ref>

==''Rings and Ideals'' (1948)==
McCoy wrote the 8th book in the series of [[Carus Mathematical Monographs]] published by the [[Mathematical Association of America]]. The book is almost entirely self-contained.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Rings and Ideals'' by N. H. McCoy|website=Bookstore, American Mathematical Society|url=https://bookstore.ams.org/car-8}}</ref> In a 1948 review, [[André Weil]] praised the book for the optimized simplicity of the mathematical proofs, an "easy and readable style", and "skillful use of examples".<ref>{{cite journal|author=Weil, André|title=review of ''Rings and Ideals'' by Neal H. McCoy|journal=Science|date=April 22, 1948|volume=109|issue=2834|page=428|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.109.2834.428.a|doi=10.1126/science.109.2834.428.a|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In a 1949 review, [[Cyrus Colton MacDuffee|C. C. MacDuffee]] praised the book — "as an introduction to the powerful and highly abstract method of thinking which now characterizes modern algebra, it is a gem."<ref>{{cite journal|author=MacDuffee, C. C.|title=Review: ''Rings and Ideals'' by N. H. McCoy|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|date=September 1949|volume=55 |issue=9 |pages=864–866|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1949-09282-0 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-55/issue-9/Review-N-H-McCoy-Rings-and-ideals/bams/1183514101.full|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1929 in Iowa, Neal H. McCoy married Ardis Hollingsworth (1904–1988). Their only son, Paul Albert McCoy, was killed in 1957 at age 22 in an automobile accident.<ref name=papers/>
